utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, Mr. Daryl Mundis, Tecla Henry-Benjamin, and Kimberly Fleming, as case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mrs. Benjamin. And the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mrs. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Mr. Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present in the courtroom, the representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence, the accused, and everyone else present in the courtroom. We'll be continuing with the examination of a witness today. But before we do so, I would like to inform you about the future hearings we will be having. As you know, a request was submitted to us concerning tendering into evidence statements in accordance with Rule 92 bis. We'll be rendering a decision about three new testimonies, so we'll have a number of written statements that will be tendered into evidence, and the Defence hasn't raised any objections to this. If you agree to this, we can tender these documents into evidence and we can have an identification number. We could do so on the 8th of April. And we have scheduled a hearing on that day for tendering exhibits into evidence, exhibits that haven't been contested. So this will be dealt with on the 8th of April, in accordance with a fairly simple procedure. I'll indicate the name of the person who testified, the reference to the articles in the indictment that concern the testimony, and I will ask the registrar to give these documents a number. And then we will examine all these documents. As you know, these documents will no longer be the subject of discussion because the Defence hasn't requested cross-examination. But these documents have to be tendered into evidence after having been given a number. This will be done on the 8th of April. Mr. Withopf isn't present, but his colleagues could inform him about what I said with regard to tendering documents into evidence on the 8th of April. It would be good if the Prosecution put these exhibits in a binder so that each Judge can have his own binder and so that the representatives of the Defence also have their own binders. So each exhibit would be in a binder, and this would facilitate matters, because then when reference is made to a document, it can be found in the binders. A binder should also be provided to the registrar on the 8th of April, which is when we will be giving these exhibits numbers. This has been done in a number of Trial Chambers. There shouldn't be any technical difficulties. And this will make things easier. And when it is the Defence's turn, if necessary the Defence can also consult its binders when these documents are referred to. It won't be necessary for them to search for those documents all over the place. So I just wanted to provide you with this information that should facilitate everyone's work. In addition, there's one last matter, a minor matter, which is a practical issue, and it concerns the Prosecution. It also seems to be a good idea that when the Prosecution calls witnesses, if it is calling important witnesses, it would be best for them to appear on Monday or Tuesday, rather than at the end of the week. Because if they have to continue with the witness's testimony, that will make it necessary for the witness to stay over the weekend. We saw that in a previous case. So this is just a technical matter, but in the case of important witnesses it might be good for everyone if these witnesses appeared at the beginning of the week. In the case of expert witnesses who will be testifying over a number of days, it would be best for the witness -- for the expert witness to appear at the beginning of the week, rather than appearing on Thursday, because in that case the witness might have to continue testifying on Monday. So this concerns the Prosecution, but it could also concern the Defence when the Defence calls important witnesses. Yet again, it would be best for them to appear at the beginning of the week, rather than at the end of the week. Could the usher now lower the blinds so that we can call the witness into the courtroom. I have another point to raise: We could have had this hearing this morning, as the courtroom was available. I'll turn to the Prosecution now, but I think that the situation will be the same tomorrow, so it would be possible for us to have the hearing in the morning, rather than at the beginning of the afternoon. But all this depends on the Prosecution. It depends on whether they have to see their witness before or not. So this is a question I am putting to the Prosecution. They can think about it and perhaps inform us whether this would be possible. If the registrar can confirm that the courtroom is available tomorrow, and if this doesn't cause any problems for the Defence, we could consider this. We'll address the matter again at the end of the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, madam. Can you hear what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: are to your left, will now proceed with their cross-examination. Naturally, if there are any questions that might reveal the identity of the witness, in that case you should ask us to go into private session. But I'm going to ask the registrar to prepare an order to redact the term that I used with regard to the witness. It's in line 25; page 4, line 25, that's where the term appears.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go into private session for the first few questions I have to ask. Could we go into private session for the first few questions I have to ask.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that Gornji Cukle is a village in which Muslims and Croats lived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The village was divided into Gornji and Donji Cukle, upper and lower Cukle; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You personally lived in Gornji Cukle.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslim villages were in -- the Muslim houses were in the middle of the village and were surrounded by Croatian houses; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Croatian village was a little further up, and yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Around the village of Cukle, there were the villages of Ovnak, Susanj, and Grahovcici, which were also Croatian villages.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ovnak is about 2 kilometres from Gornji Cukle as the crow flies; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The village of Grahovcici is a little further away; it is about 3 to 4 kilometres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The village of Sarici is even further; it's about 5 kilometres from Gornji Cukle; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But it's on the other side of the river.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All these villages that I have mentioned are Croatian villages inhabited by Croats; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, Gornji Cukle was surrounded by these Croatian villages.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness ZD, would it be correct to say that at the beginning of the war the Croatian population from your hamlet of Bare had already started digging trenches for the protection of the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go up there. They're a little further away from my house. I am not aware of them digging trenches. I don't know why they'd do that. I didn't hear anything about that. To be quite frank, I didn't hear about that. There were barely five or six men there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. If you don't know anything about it, you don't have to answer the question. Is it correct to say that the inhabitants who were members of the HVO also dug trenches at the position in Ustica [phoen] and they also faced Gornji Cukle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't face Gornji Cukle. It was a sort of protection. They were always hoping for some sort of army to arrive from the mountain.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would it also be correct to say that the HVO had a checkpoint and a fortification on Ovnak itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. It was up there on Ovnak. And the Muslim side had this on all the other sides. So you couldn't approach Zenica. You couldn't approach Travnik. Muslims had their own.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You spoke about that yesterday. Are you aware of the fact that members of the army from Gornji Cukle, for a certain period of time before the conflict, weren't able to pass through those checkpoints in order to go to the lines facing the Serbian positions in Vlasic? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they all went together until people were disarmed at Zukica Most, those members who were coming back from the Serbian positions. They were disarmed, and they took their weapons. And then our people --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And then the HVO didn't allow the BH army members to pass through either.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. All of the worst things happened very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now let's talk about the day you have mentioned. You said that when you heard the shooting and realised that it was an attack, you withdrew to Vran.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's an area a little below. Vran was above. But I was a little lower. There was a house, a Croatian house. And that's where we went. There was a forest and a cave there, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, you and your mother-in-law and some children and some locals withdrew and took shelter in a cave called Medvedja Spilja, the bear's cave.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a cave. There were some rocks there. You could shelter there. You could shelter there from the rain. Later it started raining very hard, so yes, that's where we concealed ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to ask you about. While you were there, it started raining very hard outside.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It started raining. And as the army was passing through --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Medvedja Spilja, in Vran, is about 1 and a half to 2 kilometres from Gornji Cukle; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not even that much. When you have a look, it's a little further up. Everything here is connected. This was just a little bit elevated. The road was further down below, but you could see everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You could see the village from there, as you have just described, but you can't see anything in the village and you can't hear what the people in the village said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard everything; we could see everything. I am telling you, madam, as I was there and I saw everything, we could understand everything. We could understand what was being said.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The village of Sarici, which is on the other side, 5 kilometres away, in that village you were only able to see the houses.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we could see the houses. It's elevated, so you can see it from far away.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Everything that you saw there -- all that you saw there was just the smoke that you could see after some houses had been shelled.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were houses on fire. It had all been set on fire. You could see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But on that day, when you had a look from the cave, all you could see was that after it had been shelled there was smoke rising from some of the houses. That's what you saw on that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was on that day and on the following day, until the village was razed to the ground. That's what happened every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From that place, all you could see were the houses in Grahovcici, which was a few kilometres away from you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the afternoon, we went to the other side and we could see it a little better. We could see Grahovcici a little better. When we set off in the afternoon, we could see Ovnak and Grahovcici a little better, when it was already dark.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From the places where you were and the places you passed through, you could only see these villages and houses from a distance, and in the village in Grahovcici and in Sarici you couldn't see any of the people; it was too far away.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't see any of the people there, but I know who attacked those villages. It was established that the army attacked them and that they were in the surroundings at the time, but no, I won't say that I could see that over there. I didn't see anything until I went into my village and saw people, met people, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The houses that were on fire that you saw burning, they only started burning after the villages had been shelled.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after the villages had been shelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Witness ZD. On the following day, you said that BH army soldiers took you to your village, and after having described everything that you described, you were put in a garage.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But we tried to surrender to the soldiers. Vera Zabic is unfortunately dead now, but we first tried to surrender, and then we got down there --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, after that event, you were placed in this garage.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in a house first of all in Bare. They first placed us in a house. My children were separated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After having been placed in that house, they placed you in the garage.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When it was already about 10.00 in the evening, that's when they took us out and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This garage is right by the road that goes through the village.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's by the road itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: There's a water pump by the garage itself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the lower side of the garage, there's a water pump.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And to the left and to the right --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The garage is down there, the house further up, and the water pump was between.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: By the garage itself, both to the left and to the right, there was a house and a stables.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a wall down there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Above the road, across the road from the garage, there was a big house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a big house, Mehmed Softic's house. It was one of the most beautiful houses there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From the garage and in front of the garage, when you went to wash, you weren't able to see the village of Sarici because of these houses. You weren't able to see the village you could see from the Medvedja cave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could see everything if you looked. But we heard shooting. We heard people rejoicing by the garage itself when the house was set on fire. We could hear conversations. We could hear everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From that place by the garage and in the garage, all you could hear were the voices, but you couldn't see anything; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't even say that we saw something. When we were outside, we could see things. We spent two days observing when we were in the woods. We were in the woods for two days, and on the third day we went down into the village. But we were walking around the woods for two days.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mrs. ZD, is it correct to say that in fact you never saw Commander Mehmed Alagic, you didn't see him personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, Mehmed Alagic was there. He was in that house. Because a soldier said, "We're looking after him." And later, when I saw that panic was spread, I asked a soldier to take me to see him so that I could ask for help. He only laughed and said, "Everything will be fine."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't see him personally.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him personally. I saw him later in Zenica in the newspapers. Mr. Alija congratulated him. A neighbour brought some newspapers. So I saw him in the newspapers. That's how it was. And later, on the television.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But I don't -- you will agree with me if I say that Mehmed Alagic neither during the war or after the war came to Gornji Cukle.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did come. He went to Guca Gora too. Let me tell you. I heard about this from a man of ours. He was captured by our people, but they released him. Our people had captured him, but they released him. Between the conflict, about two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness ZD. You personally didn't see how your husband was killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that myself. He died by Lukovic Omer's house. They were digging a trench. Others were preparing things. No one could do anything. They could kill whoever they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Madam ZD, that your husband and your sons, as members of the HVO, having been killed, the family of killed veterans enjoys certain benefits today, a pension, disability allowance, and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam ZD.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you have anything else to ask me, I'm ready to tell you everything I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I would have a question for you, madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following your reply, when you commented on what you saw from the position in the cave, the Defence asked you on several occasions what you saw, the burning houses, that this was due to shelling. That is the Defence that used this term; it wasn't you. And in the LiveNote, the English word is "shelling." For you, those houses that were burning, were they set on fire or were they burning because they were shelled with mortars? Because "shelling" means that mortar fire was opened at them. So what would you say regarding those burning houses? Were they set on fire or something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the army entered the village of Bare, that house, they set it on fire to celebrate their arrival there. And afterwards we could hear through the loudspeaker that they gave instructions not to set fire to the houses any longer, that they were full of everything, they needed to be saved and looted. I heard that, and I would be ready to take a solemn oath before God about that. I only told you what I heard and saw. As for those that started burning from shelling, that's something else. But as they looted the houses, then they told us to leave Bare and then they looted. But anyway, everything was burnt down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're telling us that There were two things: First, there were people who set fire to houses; and then there was also shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those that burnt during the fighting, during the shelling. But afterwards, there was no more shelling. And when the people left the houses, there was nothing to shell. And they burnt my son's house too a day later. His next-door neighbour, he wouldn't let a woman enter, and when they had taken everything out of the house, they set fire to it, my son's house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I turn to the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We have no questions for this witness. In the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, the Prosecution indicated that this witness would only testify about incidents that were not relevant to their case against Mr. Kubura, and that is indeed how the testimony has turned out, so we have nothing to ask this witness. I'm grateful, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dixon. I turn now to Ms. Benjamin to ask her whether she has any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, will you please prepare an order for me, as we are in open session, for the redaction -- no. Actually, in the translation, it didn't appear, but it did in the French translation. I heard something. So it's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Out of precaution, it would be desirable to redact line 22 on page 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, Ms. Benjamin. Put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, do you think we need to go into private session? I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you believe that the question might identify the witness, it would be preferable.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Out of abundance of caution, I think we better go into private session, just in case she --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 26th day of February, 2004, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.13 p.m.,
